Will I live to see the de-Nathanization of Germany?

A great encounter with land and sea at Cape Finisterre. A great encounter with the Vandals through Christian Courtois’s book Les Vandales (1955). Gelimer’s laughter, la carcajada de Gelimer, and the smiles of Daniel and the Evangelist John in the Pórtico de la Gloria at Santiago.
Perhaps nothing remains to us but Gelimer’s laughter. But the smiles of Daniel and the Evangelist follow me into my dreams.
Two attempts were suppressed and quickly smothered:

And now, in 1958, the third attempt: the collected essays and the commemorative volume.
Only a born counterfeiter could have come up with the idea of the three rings in Nathan the Wise.

“In proud admiration I compared the rise of the Reich with the slow decline of the Austrian state.”

The night before: an encounter with the princeps religiosissimus, the most religious prince, Sisebut; with the Lecto de la validez—the validity of a baptism once it has been carried out—and with the validez del Lecto.
Vitoria later treated the matter in exactly the same way.
The scandal has already happened. To undo it would create a new scandal. So the baptism performed by force remains valid.
He was forced, but he willed it.
Long live the pious King Sisebut!
Long live Innocent III and his decretal Maiores!
Long live Canon 57 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and Gratian’s gloss on C. 5 D. XLV!
The concept of scandal as the great back door of jurisprudence based on the concrete situation!
Against a pirate, a pirate and a half!
Against a Jew, a Jew and a half!
Secundum occasionem et veritatem coactus sive condicionaliter, sive absolute voluit.

According to the circumstances and the truth of the matter, although he was forced, he nevertheless willed it—whether conditionally or absolutely. Here lies the true source and practical end result of all Vitoria’s beautiful arguments in De Indis, and of his supposed founding of modern international law.

On the note from the end of 1956, at the top of p. 80 [= pp. 353 ff.]:
De Gaulle is only an interlude. He is catching up with Germany.
Much will still be repeated elsewhere that we in Germany got ahead of everyone in doing first.
Until then, we remain the people of collective shame, and we introduce Days of Shame as paid public holidays:
a Devil’s Calendar instead of a Calendar of Saints.
So God is the Wholly Other.
That is exactly what human beings need in order to become human. Alienation, then, is not an objection and it is not a refutation.

Human beings need something of this kind in order to estrange themselves from the animal and become human. But there are also false forms of alienation. And those, naturally, are deadly. Then begins the hopeless struggle over what is genuine and what is false—which means friend and enemy—with all its satanic violence and all its Nathan-like fraud.
The destruction of genuineness as such!
Today, survivors are reproached for having survived.
Ernst Jünger reproached me for exactly this in January 1950.
What does that mean in legal terms?
It means that certain people claim the right to survive for themselves while denying that same right to others.
Why did you not throw yourself onto the tyrant’s knife?
Well, did you throw yourself onto his knife?
But I did not support him!
Everyone who lived through the period supported him in some way—even everyone who tried to assassinate him.
I am eager to read Jünger’s new diary from the occupation years.
I reread what he wrote in 1950, in his letters of 10 and 16 January:
“Had you followed my advice and example in this matter, you might no longer be alive today, but you would have the right to pass final judgment on me.”
So that is his court-of-last-resort relationship to me!
And yet he has not read a single one of my legal works. Encased in his own armor, he has never even felt the slightest impulse to find out what I actually wrote in that field.
And now I am supposed to send him my collection of essays on constitutional law?
So that I can be told that I had no right to survive?
That would amount to submitting to his claim to pronounce death sentences simply by treating a person’s survival as something to hold against him.
Gelimer’s laughter is still the mildest possible answer to insults as deadly as these.
